preamble.summary: Ben Sira warns against presuming on wealth, self-sufficiency, or God's patience. Do not say 'I will sin and God will forgive' -- divine mercy is not a license for recklessness. The second half is devoted to the ethics of speech: be swift to hear and slow to answer, do not spread slander, guard your tongue, and let your words be consistent and truthful.
preamble.remarkable: The warning against presumptuous reliance on God's mercy (vv. 4-7) directly addresses the theological complacency that later Christian writers called 'cheap grace.' The speech-ethics section (vv. 11-18) is among the most developed in the wisdom tradition and anticipates James 3:1-12 in its concern with the destructive power of the tongue.
preamble.friction: The assertion that God's wrath 'comes suddenly' (v. 7) creates tension with the patience theology of chapter 2. Ben Sira manages both truths -- God is patient AND God's judgment can arrive without warning -- without fully synthesizing them.
preamble.connections: Romans 2:4-5 (presuming on God's kindness); James 3:1-12 (the tongue as fire); Proverbs 10:19 (in many words sin is not absent); Ecclesiastes 5:1-2 (be not rash with your mouth); Psalm 62:10 (do not trust in wealth).

verses.text_latin: Noli adtendere ad possessiones iniquas et ne dixeris est mihi sufficiens vitae multae enim divitiae sunt mihi.
verses.rendering: Do not set your heart on ill-gotten possessions, and do not say, 'I have enough for my life,' for great riches are mine.
translator_notes: The chapter opens by targeting the wealthy who feel self-sufficient. The danger is not wealth per se but the false security it breeds.

key_terms.note: Iniquus marks the wealth as unjustly acquired; the warning applies to both the means of acquisition and the attitude of possession.

verses.text_latin: Ne sequaris concupiscentiam et fortitudinem tuam.
verses.rendering: Do not follow your desire and your strength.
translator_notes: Concupiscentia paired with fortitudo: the combination of wanting and having the power to get is particularly dangerous.

key_terms.note: Concupiscentia here is disordered appetite generally, not yet the narrow sexual sense it acquired in later Latin theology.

verses.text_latin: Et ne dixeris quomodo potui aut quis me subiciet propter facta mea Deus enim vindicans vindicabit.
verses.rendering: And do not say, 'Who can overpower me?' or 'Who will hold me accountable for my deeds?' For God will surely take vengeance.
translator_notes: The arrogant question 'Who can overpower me?' echoes Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, and other proud rulers who learned the answer too late.

key_terms.note: The doubled verb (Hebrew infinitive absolute construction preserved in Latin) intensifies certainty: God will without fail repay.

verses.text_latin: Ne dixeris peccavi et quid mihi accidit triste Altissimus enim est patiens redditor.
verses.rendering: Do not say, 'I sinned, and what harm came to me?' For the Most High is a patient recompenser.
translator_notes: The most dangerous presumption: interpreting God's patience as indifference. Ben Sira warns that divine forbearance has a limit.

key_terms.note: God is patient (patiens) but also one who repays (redditor); patience does not cancel justice.

verses.text_latin: De propitiato peccato noli esse sine metu neque adicias peccatum super peccatum.
verses.rendering: Concerning forgiven sin, do not be without fear, and do not heap sin upon sin.
translator_notes: Forgiveness received should produce grateful vigilance, not careless repetition.

key_terms.note: From propitiare, to appease or make favorable; the sin has been covered but the inclination to repeat it remains.

verses.text_latin: Et ne dixeris miseratio Domini magna est multitudinis peccatorum meorum miserebitur.
verses.rendering: And do not say, 'His mercy is great; he will forgive the multitude of my sins.'
translator_notes: This is the classic statement of presumption: using the doctrine of mercy as a pretext for continued sinning. It was a central proof-text in Catholic moral theology against the vice of praesumptio.

key_terms.note: Miseratio is the emotional dimension of mercy -- compassion, pity -- as distinct from misericordia, which adds the element of active response.

verses.text_latin: Misericordia enim et ira ab illo cito proximant et in peccatores respicit ira illius.
verses.rendering: For mercy and wrath alike come swiftly from him, and his anger rests upon sinners.
translator_notes: The parallelism is deliberate: mercy and wrath are not opposites but twin aspects of God's engagement with humanity. Both can arrive 'swiftly' (cito).

key_terms.note: Ira Dei (the wrath of God) is not capricious anger but the just response of holiness to persistent rebellion.

verses.text_latin: Non tardes converti ad Dominum et ne differas de die in diem.
verses.rendering: Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day.
translator_notes: The urgency of repentance: delay is itself a form of presumption.

key_terms.note: Conversio is the Latin rendering of Hebrew teshuvah (return/repentance); it implies a complete reorientation of life.

verses.text_latin: Subito enim veniet ira illius et in tempore vindictae disperdet te.
verses.rendering: For his wrath will come suddenly, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you.
translator_notes: 'Subito' (suddenly) is the key word: the sinner who delays assumes time is available, but judgment may strike without warning.

verses.text_latin: Noli anxius esse in divitiis iniustis non enim proderunt tibi in die obductionis et vindictae.
verses.rendering: Do not be anxious about unjust riches, for they will profit you nothing in the day of adversity and vengeance.
translator_notes: Returns to the opening theme: unjust wealth is useless when divine judgment arrives.

verses.text_latin: Non ventiles te in omnem ventum et non eas in omnem viam sic enim omnis peccator probatur in duplici lingua.
verses.rendering: Do not winnow yourself in every wind, and do not walk in every path; for so is every sinner tested who speaks with a double tongue.
translator_notes: The winnowing image is agricultural: grain tossed in every breeze scatters uselessly. The 'double tongue' connects speech to moral instability.

key_terms.note: Parallels the 'double heart' of 1:37 and 2:15; in speech, duplicity means saying one thing and meaning another.

verses.text_latin: Esto firmus in via Domini et in veritate sensus tui et scientia et prosequatur te verbum pacis et iustitiae.
verses.rendering: Be steadfast in the way of the Lord, and in the truth of your understanding and knowledge, and let the word of peace and justice attend you.

verses.text_latin: Esto mansuetus ad audiendum verbum ut intellegas et cum sapientia proferas verum responsum.
verses.rendering: Be gentle in hearing a word, so that you may understand, and with wisdom give a true answer.
translator_notes: Listening precedes speaking; understanding precedes answering. This is the core discipline of wise speech.

key_terms.note: The gentle listener is receptive and unhurried, the opposite of the impulsive speaker.

verses.text_latin: Si est tibi intellectus responde proximo sin autem sit manus tua super os tuum ne capiaris in verbo indisciplinato et confundaris.
verses.rendering: If you have understanding, answer your neighbor; but if not, let your hand be over your mouth, lest you be caught in an undisciplined word and put to shame.
translator_notes: The image of the hand over the mouth is found also in Job 21:5 and 40:4; it represents the physical discipline of silence.

verses.text_latin: Honor et gloria in sermone sensati lingua vero imprudentis subversio est ipsius.
verses.rendering: Honor and glory are in the speech of the discerning, but the tongue of the fool is his own ruin.

verses.text_latin: Non appelleris susurro et lingua tua ne capiaris et confundaris.
verses.rendering: Do not be called a whisperer, and do not be caught and put to shame by your tongue.

key_terms.note: The susurro is a gossip or slanderer who speaks in undertones; the word itself sounds like whispering.

verses.text_latin: Super furem enim est confusio et paenitentia et denotatio pessima super bilinguem susurroni autem odium et inimicitia et contumelia.
verses.rendering: For upon the thief fall shame and reproach, and the worst disgrace upon the double-tongued; but upon the whisperer fall hatred, enmity, and insult.
translator_notes: The hierarchy of social censure: the thief loses honor, the two-faced person loses reputation, the gossip loses relationships entirely.

key_terms.note: Bilinguis (two-tongued) is one who says different things to different people; a more specific form of duplici corde.

verses.rendering: Treat the small and the great alike with justice.
translator_notes: The chapter closes with a lapidary command for impartial justice, forming an inclusio with the opening warning against unjust wealth.

key_terms.note: Iustificare here means to render a just verdict or fair treatment, not the theological sense of 'declare righteous.'
